about: THE CHEST'S TEXTS - real texts of 793-1066 (or told of it, written down later: toldLater), each in its own tongue with a free translation that passes the rule (the translator died in 1955 or before, published before 1931), with where it is found and a credit line. Made by Bake/guide/make_chest_data.py from the research in Plans/environment_research/m2. Readings added 4 Oct 2026 by Bake/guide/make_readings.py: Beowulf (43 fitts), The Seafarer, The Wanderer, Deor, Maldon, Hávamál stanzas, Ælfric's merchant, the Saxon vow, Alcuin 793, the 793 annal, the Irish Viking quatrain; entries with check=true carry an original quoted from memory to be checked; ownTranslation=true marks the game's own drafts for the user to edit.

texts.title: Gestumblindi's riddle 1
texts.original:
Hafa ek þat vilda es ek hafða í gær;
vittu hvat þat vas:
Lýða lemill, ok orða tefill,
ok orða upp-hefill?
Heiðrekr konungr hygg þú at gꜵ́to!
texts.translation: Would I had what I had yesterday! guess thou what it was: Men’s damager, words’ hinderer, and yet words’ arouser. Read my riddle, O King Heidrek!
texts.translator: Gudbrand Vigfusson (d. 1889) and F. York Powell (d. 1904)
texts.where: Corpus Poeticum Boreale vol. 1 (1883), Bk II §1 King Heidrek's Riddles, no. 1, p. 87 (ll. 1-5); IA corpuspoeticumbo01guuoft page n222; scratchpad/cpb1.txt lines 15679-15683 (Norse), 15699-15705 (English). Norse read from the page image (the OCR garbles þ, ð, ꜵ).

texts.title: Gestumblindi's riddle 2
texts.original:
Heiman ek fór, heiman ek fær gœrðag,
sá-ek á veg vega:
vegr vas undir, ok vegr yfir,
ok vegr á alla vega?—Heiðr. k. h.
texts.translation: I came from home, I wended my way from home, I saw a way of ways; way underneath, way above head, way on all sides. Read my, etc.
texts.translator: Gudbrand Vigfusson (d. 1889) and F. York Powell (d. 1904)

texts.title: Gestumblindi's riddle 3
texts.original:
Hvat-es þat drykkja es ek drakk í gœr;
vasa þat vín né vatn,
miꜵðr né mungát, né matar ekki,
þó gekk ek þorsta-lauss þaðan?—H. k. h.
texts.translation: What drink was it I drank yesterday; it was neither wine nor water, nor mead, nor beer, nor aught of meat kind; yet I went thirstless away? Read my, etc.
texts.translator: Gudbrand Vigfusson (d. 1889) and F. York Powell (d. 1904)

texts.title: Gestumblindi's riddle 4
texts.original:
Hverr es sá inn hvelli es gengr harðar gꜵtor
ok hefir hann þær fyrr of farit:
miꜵk fast kyssir ok hefir munna tvá,
sá es á golli eino gengr?—H. k. h.
texts.translation: Who is that shrill one, who walks by hard paths, having passed them many a time; he kisses very fast, has two mouths, walks on nought but gold? Read my, etc.
texts.translator: Gudbrand Vigfusson (d. 1889) and F. York Powell (d. 1904)

texts.title: Gestumblindi's riddle 5
texts.original:
Hverr es sá inn mikli es ferr mold yfir,
svelgr hann vꜵtn ok við,
glygg hann oask enn guma eigi,
ok yrkir á sól til saka?—H. k. h.
texts.translation: Who is the huge one, who passes over the earth, swallowing water and woods; he fears the wind, but no man, and wages war on the sun? Read my, etc.
texts.translator: Gudbrand Vigfusson (d. 1889) and F. York Powell (d. 1904)

texts.title: Gestumblindi's riddle 6
texts.original:
Hverr es sá inn mikli es mar veðr,
ok horfir til Heljar halfr;
ꜵldom hann bergr, enn við iꜵrð sakask,
ef hann hefir ser vel trausta við?—H. k. h.
texts.translation: Who is the big one, who wades in the deep, turning half towards Hell; he saves people, but tugs against the earth, if he has a trusty withy by him? Read my, etc.
texts.translator: Gudbrand Vigfusson (d. 1889) and F. York Powell (d. 1904)

texts.title: Gestumblindi's riddle 7
texts.original:
Hverr byggir há fiꜵll? Hverr fellr í diúpa dala?
hverr anda-lauss lifir?
hverr æva þegir?—H. k. h.
texts.translation: Who dwells in high mountains? Who falls into deep dales? Who lives without breath? Who is never silent? Read my, etc.
texts.translator: Gudbrand Vigfusson (d. 1889) and F. York Powell (d. 1904)

texts.title: Gestumblindi's riddle 8
texts.original:
Hvat es þat undra es ek úti ság
fyr Dellings durom:
Hꜵfði síno vísar Heljar til,
enn fótom til sólar snýr?—H. k. h.
texts.translation: What was that wonder I saw outside Delling’s door (outside the hall): It turns its head towards Hell, and its feet towards the Sun? Read my, etc.
texts.translator: Gudbrand Vigfusson (d. 1889) and F. York Powell (d. 1904)

texts.title: Gestumblindi's riddle 9
texts.original:
Hvat es þat undra es ek úti ság
fyr Dellings durom:
Ókyrrir tveir anda-lausir
sára-lauk suðo?—H. k. h.
texts.translation: What was that wonder, etc.: Two ever-stirring yet lifeless things were boiling a wound-leek? Read my, etc.
texts.translator: Gudbrand Vigfusson (d. 1889) and F. York Powell (d. 1904)

texts.title: Gestumblindi's riddle 10
texts.original:
Hvat es þat undra es ek úti ság
fyr Dellings durom:
Hvítir fliúgendr hello liósta,
enn svartir í sand grafask?—H. k. h.
texts.translation: What was that wonder, etc.: The white flyers beat the rock, while the black ones are embedded in the sand? Read my, etc.
texts.translator: Gudbrand Vigfusson (d. 1889) and F. York Powell (d. 1904)

texts.title: Gestumblindi's riddle 11
texts.original:
Hvat es þat undra es ek úti ság
fyr Dellings durom:
Svartan gꜵlt ek sá í sauri vaða,
ok reisat honom burst á baki?—H. k. h.
texts.translation: What was that wonder, etc.: I saw a black hog wallow in the mud, though no bristles were on his back? Read my, etc.
texts.translator: Gudbrand Vigfusson (d. 1889) and F. York Powell (d. 1904)

texts.title: Gestumblindi's riddle 12
texts.original:
Hvat es þat undra es ek úti ság
fyr Dellings durom:
tio hefir tungor, tuttugo augo,
fióra tigo fóta, fram líðr sú vættr?—H. k. h.
texts.translation: What was that wonder, etc.: It has ten tongues, twenty eyes, forty feet; this being moves along? Read my, etc.
texts.translator: Gudbrand Vigfusson (d. 1889) and F. York Powell (d. 1904)

texts.title: Gestumblindi's riddle 13
texts.original:
Hvat es þat undra es ek úti ság
fyr Dellings durom:
Ofarliga flýgr, ‘arn-hlióð’ gellr,
‘harðar ro hilmir’ . . .?—H. k. h.
texts.translation: What was that wonder, etc.: It flies high aloft, yelling loud . . . .? Read my, etc.
texts.translator: Gudbrand Vigfusson (d. 1889) and F. York Powell (d. 1904)

texts.title: Gestumblindi's riddle 14
texts.original:
Hvat es þat undra es ek úti ság
fyr Dellings durom:
Fœ́tr hefir átta en fiogor augo,
berr þat ofar kné an kvið?—H. k. h.
texts.translation: What was that wonder, etc.: It has eight feet, four eyes, carrying its knees higher than its belly? Read my, etc.
texts.translator: Gudbrand Vigfusson (d. 1889) and F. York Powell (d. 1904)

texts.title: Gestumblindi's riddle 15
texts.original:
Hvat es þat undra es ek úti ság
fyr Dellings durom:
lýðom lýsir lꜵnd ꜵll yfir,
ok keppask um þat vargar of-allt?—H. k. h.
texts.translation: What was that wonder, etc.: It lightens people over all lands, and yet is ever chased by wolves? Read my, etc.
texts.translator: Gudbrand Vigfusson (d. 1889) and F. York Powell (d. 1904)
texts.where: CPB vol. 1 (1883) p. 89, riddle 15 (ll. 57-60); IA corpuspoeticumbo01guuoft n224; cpb1.txt lines 15819-15822 (Norse), 15851-15852 (English)

texts.title: Gestumblindi's riddle 16
texts.original:
Hvat es þat undra es ek úti ság
fyr Dellings durom:
horni harðara, hrafni svartara,
skialli hvítara, skapti réttara?—H. k. h.
texts.translation: What was that wonder, etc.: Harder than horn, blacker than a raven, whiter than egg-film, straighter than a shaft? Read my, etc.
texts.translator: Gudbrand Vigfusson (d. 1889) and F. York Powell (d. 1904)

texts.title: Gestumblindi's riddle 17
texts.original:
Bꜵ́ro brúðir bleik-haddaðar,
ambáttir tvær, ꜵl til skemmo;
vasat þat hꜵndom horfit, né hꜵmrom klappat,
þó es fyr eyjar útan ꜵrðigr [es] ker gœrði?—H. k. h.
texts.translation: Blond-haired brides, bondswomen both, carried ale to the barn; the casks were not turned with hands, nor forged by hammers; she that made it strutted about outside the isles? Read my, etc.
texts.translator: Gudbrand Vigfusson (d. 1889) and F. York Powell (d. 1904)

texts.title: Gestumblindi's riddle 18
texts.original:
Hverjar ro þær rygjar á regin-fialli,
elr við kvꜵ́n kona:
mær við meyjo mꜵg of getr;
ok eigot þær varðir vera?—H. k. h.
texts.translation: Who are those fairies of the mighty mountains; woman begets by a woman; a maid bears a son by a maid. Those goodwives have no husband? Read my, etc.
texts.translator: Gudbrand Vigfusson (d. 1889) and F. York Powell (d. 1904)

texts.title: Gestumblindi's riddle 19
texts.original:
Hverjar ro drósir es um sínn dróttinn
vápn-lausar vega:
enar iꜵrpo hlífa alla daga,
enn enar fegri fara?—H. k. h.
texts.translation: Who are the maids that fight weaponless around their lord; the brown ever sheltering, the fair ever attacking him? Read my, etc.
texts.translator: Gudbrand Vigfusson (d. 1889) and F. York Powell (d. 1904)

texts.title: Gestumblindi's riddle 20
texts.original:
Hverjar ro þær leikor es líða lꜵnd yfir
at fꜵgnuði fꜵðor:
hvítan skiꜵld þær á vetrom betra,
enn svartan um sumar?—H. k. h.
texts.translation: Who are the merry maids that glide above the land to the joy of their father; in winter they bear a white shield, but black in summer? Read my, etc.
texts.translator: Gudbrand Vigfusson (d. 1889) and F. York Powell (d. 1904)

texts.title: Gestumblindi's riddle 21
texts.original:
Hverjar ro þær snótir es ganga syrgjandi
at fꜵgnuði fꜵðor:
hadda bleika hafa þær enar hvít-fꜵldnu,
ok eigo í vindi vaka?—H. k. h.
texts.translation: Who are the maids that go weeping to the joy of their father, white-hooded, fair-haired, wide awake in a gale? Read my, etc.
texts.translator: Gudbrand Vigfusson (d. 1889) and F. York Powell (d. 1904)

texts.title: Gestumblindi's riddle 22
texts.original:
Hverjar ro þær meyjar es margar ganga saman
at fꜵgnuði fꜵðor:
mꜵrgom hafa manni þær at meini komit,
ok eigot þær varðir vera?—H. k. h.
texts.translation: Who are the maids that go many together to the joy of their father; they have brought grief to many; these goodwives have no husbands? Read my, etc.
texts.translator: Gudbrand Vigfusson (d. 1889) and F. York Powell (d. 1904)

texts.title: Gestumblindi's riddle 23
texts.original:
Hverjar ro þær brúðir es ganga brim-skerjom í,
ok eigo eptir firði fꜵr:
harðan beð hafa þær enar hvít-fꜵldno,
ok leika í logni fátt?—H. k. h.
texts.translation: Who are the brides that walk over the reefs, and drive along the friths; these white-hooded ladies have a hard bed; in calm weather they make no stir? Read my, etc.
texts.translator: Gudbrand Vigfusson (d. 1889) and F. York Powell (d. 1904)

texts.title: Gestumblindi's riddle 24
texts.original:
Fara ek ság foldar mold-bua,
ok sat nár á ná;
blindr reið blindom ‘brim-reiðar til,’
iór es andar-vani?—H. k. h.
texts.translation: I saw an earth-dweller pass by, a corpse sitting on a corpse; a blind one riding on a blind sea-car, yet the steed was lifeless? Read my, etc.
texts.translator: Gudbrand Vigfusson (d. 1889) and F. York Powell (d. 1904)

texts.title: Gestumblindi's riddle 25
texts.original:
Hvat es þat dýra es drepr fé manna,
ok es iarni kringt:
horn hefir átta en hꜵfuð ekki
ok . . . . . . . . .?—H. k. h.
texts.translation: What is that beast, all girdled with iron, which kills the flocks; it has eight horns, but no head, and . . . .? Read my, etc.
texts.translator: Gudbrand Vigfusson (d. 1889) and F. York Powell (d. 1904)

texts.title: Gestumblindi's riddle 26
texts.original:
Hvat es þat dýra es Dꜵnom hlífir,
berr blóðugt bak, en bergr firom,
geirom mœ́tir, gefr líf sumom;
leggr við lófa lík sítt gumi?—H. k. h.
texts.translation: What is that beast that shelters the Danes; with bloody back it covers men, encounters spears, saves many a life, fitting its body to the hands of men? Read my, etc.
texts.translator: Gudbrand Vigfusson (d. 1889) and F. York Powell (d. 1904)
texts.where: CPB vol. 1 (1883) p. 91, riddle 26 (ll. 101-104); IA corpuspoeticumbo01guuoft n226; cpb1.txt lines 15954-15957 (Norse), 15984-15986 (English)

texts.title: Gestumblindi's riddle 27
texts.original:
‘Miꜵk vas forðom nꜵsgas’ varin
barn-giꜵrn su-es bar bú-timbr saman;
hlífðo henni halms bit-skalmir,
þó lá drykkjar dryn-hraun yfir?—H. k. h.
texts.translation: A . . . . yearning for children, gathered her building materials, straw-choppers fenced her in, whilst above her was drink’s echoing hall. Read my, etc.
texts.translator: Gudbrand Vigfusson (d. 1889) and F. York Powell (d. 1904)
texts.where: CPB vol. 1 (1883) p. 91, riddle 27 (ll. 105-108); IA corpuspoeticumbo01guuoft n226; cpb1.txt lines 15958-15961 (Norse), 15988-15991 (English). CPB's Final Readings (p. cxxvi; cpb1.txt line 8755) give l. 108 as 'þó lá drykkjar dryn-rann yfir?'

texts.credit: Old Norse text and English: G. Vigfusson and F. York Powell, Corpus Poeticum Boreale (Oxford, 1883)

texts.title: Gestumblindi's riddle 28
texts.original:
Fiórir ganga, fiórir hanga,
tveir veg vísa, tveir hundom verja,
einn eptir drallar ok optast óhreinn?—H. k. h.
texts.translation: Four ganging, four hanging, two showing the way, two keeping the dogs off, one ever dirty lags behind. Read my, etc.
texts.translator: Gudbrand Vigfusson (d. 1889) and F. York Powell (d. 1904)
texts.where: CPB vol. 1 (1883) p. 91, riddle 28 (ll. 109-111); IA corpuspoeticumbo01guuoft n226; cpb1.txt lines 15962-15964 (Norse), 15993-15994 (English)

texts.title: Gestumblindi's riddle 29
texts.original:
Hverr es sá inn eini es sefr í ꜵsgrua,
ok es af grióti eino gœrr:
fꜵðor né móður áat sá inn fár-giarni,
þar mun hann sínn aldr ala?—H. k. h.
texts.translation: Who is it that sleeps in the hearth, all made of stone,—a mischievous being without father or mother,—there is his lifelong abode? Read my, etc.
texts.translator: Gudbrand Vigfusson (d. 1889) and F. York Powell (d. 1904)
texts.where: CPB vol. 1 (1883) p. 91, riddle 29 (ll. 112-115); IA corpuspoeticumbo01guuoft n226; cpb1.txt lines 15965-15968 (Norse), 15996-16000 (English)

texts.title: Gestumblindi's riddle 30
texts.original:
Hest sá ek standa, hýddi meri,
dúði dyndil, drap hlaun und kvið,
or skal draga ‘ok í optað góða’ stund.—H. k. h.
texts.translation: I saw a horse, a maid whipped it, she shook a . . . .? Read my, etc.
texts.translator: Gudbrand Vigfusson (d. 1889) and F. York Powell (d. 1904)
texts.where: CPB vol. 1 (1883) p. 91, riddle 30 (ll. 116-118); IA corpuspoeticumbo01guuoft n226; cpb1.txt lines 15969-15971 (Norse), 16003-16004 (English)

texts.title: Gestumblindi's riddle 31
texts.original:
Hverir ro þeir þegnar, es ríða þingi at,
ok ero sextán saman;
lýði sína senda þeir lꜵnd yfir
at byggja ból-staði?—H. k. h.
texts.translation: Who are the champions riding to court sixteen together; they send their men far and wide to make settlements? Read my, etc.
texts.translator: Gudbrand Vigfusson (d. 1889) and F. York Powell (d. 1904)
texts.where: CPB vol. 1 (1883) p. 92, riddle 31 (ll. 119-122); IA corpuspoeticumbo01guuoft n227; cpb1.txt lines 16019-16022 (Norse), 16050-16052 (English)

texts.title: Gestumblindi's riddle 32
texts.original:
Sá-ek á sumri sól-biꜵrgom í
verðung vaka vilgi teiti:
drukko iarlar ꜵl þegjandi,
enn œ́pandi ꜵl-ker stóðo?—H. k. h.
texts.translation: I saw in summertide a household awake and merry at sunset; the gentlemen drank their beer in silence, but the ale-butt stood and screamed. Read my, etc.
texts.translator: Gudbrand Vigfusson (d. 1889) and F. York Powell (d. 1904)
texts.where: CPB vol. 1 (1883) p. 92, riddle 32 (ll. 123-126); IA corpuspoeticumbo01guuoft n227; cpb1.txt lines 16023-16026 (Norse), 16054-16056 (English)

texts.credit: Old Norse text and English: G. Vigfusson and F. York Powell, Corpus Poeticum Boreale (Oxford, 1883)

texts.title: Gestumblindi's riddle 33
texts.original:
Meyjar ek sá moldo glíkar,
vóro þeim at beðjom biꜵrg:
svartar ok sámar í sól-viðri,
enn þess at fegri es færa of sér?—H. k. h.
texts.translation: I saw certain dust-like maidens; the rocks were their bedding; they are black and swart in sunshine, but the less one can see [i. e. in the dark] the fairer they look. Read my, etc.
texts.translator: Gudbrand Vigfusson (d. 1889) and F. York Powell (d. 1904)
texts.where: CPB vol. 1 (1883) p. 92, riddle 33 (ll. 127-130); IA corpuspoeticumbo01guuoft n227; cpb1.txt lines 16027-16030 (Norse), 16058-16060 (English)

texts.title: Gestumblindi's riddle 34
texts.original:
Sá-ek a árni, egg-dauða menn
blóðs-hol bera í biörk kviðar.
texts.translation: I saw on a (see the text).
texts.translator: Gudbrand Vigfusson (d. 1889) and F. York Powell (d. 1904)
texts.where: CPB vol. 1 (1883) p. 92, riddle 34 (ll. 131-132, 'thus emendated'; the manuscripts read 'Sat eg a segli sa eg dauða menn bloðs hold bera í bork viðar (!)'); IA corpuspoeticumbo01guuoft n227; cpb1.txt lines 16031-16032 (Norse), 16062-16063 and footnotes 16080-16089 (English)

texts.title: Gestumblindi's riddle 35
texts.original:
Hverir ro þeir tveir es tio hafa fœ́tr,
augo þriú, enn einn hala?—H. k. h.
texts.translation: Who are the two that have ten feet, three eyes, one tail? Read my, etc.
texts.translator: Gudbrand Vigfusson (d. 1889) and F. York Powell (d. 1904)
texts.where: CPB vol. 1 (1883) p. 92, riddle 35 (ll. 133-134); IA corpuspoeticumbo01guuoft n227; cpb1.txt lines 16033-16034 (Norse), 16065-16066 (English)

texts.title: Gestumblindi's last question
texts.original:
Hvat mælti Óðinn í eyra Baldri
áðr hann vas á bál um borinn?
texts.translation: What did Woden whisper into Balder’s ear ere he was borne on the pyre?
texts.translator: Gudbrand Vigfusson (d. 1889) and F. York Powell (d. 1904)
texts.where: CPB vol. 1 (1883) p. 92, no. 36 (ll. 135-136; Heidrek's reply l. 137 is in the riddle's answer); IA corpuspoeticumbo01guuoft n227; cpb1.txt lines 16035-16037 (Norse), 16068-16070 (English)

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 11
texts.original:
‘Seg mér, Gagnráþr!   alls þu á golfi vill
þíns of freista frama:
hvé sá hestr heitir   es hverjan dregr
dag of dróttmǫgu?’
texts.translation:
“Speak forth now, Gagnrath,   if there from the floor
Thou wouldst thy wisdom make known:
What name has the steed   that each morn anew
The day for mankind doth draw?”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 11. English: Bellows, The Poetic Edda (1923), Project Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3157; scratchpad/bellows.txt line 4019). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 63, IA dieliederderlte00hild page n86, read from the page image.

texts.credit: English: Henry Adams Bellows, The Poetic Edda (New York, 1923). Old Norse: K. Hildebrand and H. Gering, Die Lieder der älteren Edda (Paderborn, 1904)

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 12
texts.original:
‘Skinfaxi heitir   es enn skíra dregr
dag of dróttmǫgu;
hesta baztr   þykkir meþ Hreiþgotum,
ey lýsir mǫn af mari.’
texts.translation:
“Skinfaxi is he,   the steed who for men
The glittering day doth draw;
The best of horses   to heroes he seems,
And brightly his mane doth burn.”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 12. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3166; bellows.txt line 4028). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 64, IA dieliederderlte00hild n87.

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 13
texts.original:
‘Seg þat, Gagnráþr!   alls þu á golfi vill
þíns of freista frama:
hvé sá jór heitir   es austan dregr
nǫ́tt of nýt regin?’
texts.translation:
“Speak forth now, Gagnrath,   if there from the floor
Thou wouldst thy wisdom make known:
What name has the steed   that from East anew
Brings night for the noble gods?”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 13. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3175; bellows.txt line 4036). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 64, IA dieliederderlte00hild n87.

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 14
texts.original:
‘Hrímfaxi heitir   es hverja dregr
nǫ́tt of nýt regin;
méldropa   fellir hann morgin hvern,
þaþan kømr dǫgg of dali.’
texts.translation:
“Hrimfaxi name they   the steed that anew
Brings night for the noble gods;
Each morning foam   from his bit there falls,
And thence come the dews in the dales.”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 14. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3184; bellows.txt line 4058). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 64, IA dieliederderlte00hild n87.

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 15
texts.original:
‘Seg þat, Gagnráþr!   alls þu á golfi vill
þíns of freista frama:
hvé sú ǫ́ heitir   es deilir meþ jǫtna sunum
grund auk meþ goþum?’
texts.translation:
“Speak forth now, Gagnrath,   if there from the floor
Thou wouldst thy wisdom make known:
What name has the river   that ’twixt the realms
Of the gods and the giants goes?”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 15. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3193; bellows.txt line 4066). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 64, IA dieliederderlte00hild n87.

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 16
texts.original:
‘Ifing heitir ǫ́   es deilir meþ jǫtna sunum
grund auk meþ goþum;
opin rinna   hón skal of aldrdaga,
verþrat íss á ǫ́.’
texts.translation:
“Ifing is the river   that ’twixt the realms
Of the gods and the giants goes;
For all time ever   open it flows,
No ice on the river there is.”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 16. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3202; bellows.txt line 4075). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 65, IA dieliederderlte00hild n88.

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 17
texts.original:
‘Seg þat, Gagnráþr!   alls þu á golfi vill
þíns of freista frama:
hvé sá vǫllr heitir   es finnask vígi at
Surtr ok en svǫ́su goþ?’
texts.translation:
“Speak forth now, Gagnrath,   if there from the floor
Thou wouldst thy wisdom make known:
What name has the field   where in fight shall meet
Surt and the gracious gods?”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 17. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3211; bellows.txt line 4083). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 65, IA dieliederderlte00hild n88.

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 18
texts.original:
‘Vígríþr heitir vǫllr   es finnask vígi at
Surtr ok en svǫ́su goþ;
hundraþ rasta   hann’s á hverjan veg,
sá’s þeim vǫllr vitaþr.’
texts.translation:
“Vigrith is the field   where in fight shall meet
Surt and the gracious gods;
A hundred miles   each way does it measure,
And so are its boundaries set.”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 18. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3220; bellows.txt line 4107). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 65, IA dieliederderlte00hild n88.

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 20
texts.original:
‘Seg þat et eina,   ef þitt øþi dugir
ok þú, Vafþrúþnir! vitir:
hvaþan jǫrþ of kvam   eþa upphiminn
fyrst, enn fróþi jǫtunn?’
texts.translation:
“First answer me well,   if thy wisdom avails,
And thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now:
In earliest time   whence came the earth,
Or the sky, thou giant sage?”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 20. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3238; bellows.txt line 4123). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 66, IA dieliederderlte00hild n89.

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 21
texts.original:
‘Ór Ymis holdi   vas jǫrþ of skǫpuþ
en ór beinum bjǫrg,
himinn ór hausi   ens hrímkalda jǫtuns,
en ór sveita sǽr.’
texts.translation:
“Out of Ymir’s flesh   was fashioned the earth,
And the mountains were made of his bones;
The sky from the frost-cold   giant’s skull,
And the ocean out of his blood.”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 21. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3247; bellows.txt line 4151). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 66, IA dieliederderlte00hild n89.

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 22
texts.original:
‘Seg þat annat,   ef þitt øþi dugir
ok þú, Vafþrúþnir! vitir:
hvaþan máni of kvam,   sás ferr menn yfir,
eþa sól et sama?’
texts.translation:
“Next answer me well,   if thy wisdom avails,
And thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now:
Whence came the moon,   o’er the world of men
That fares, and the flaming sun?”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 22. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3256; bellows.txt line 4159). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 66, IA dieliederderlte00hild n89.

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 23
texts.original:
‘Mundilferi heitir,   hann es Mána faþir
ok svá Sólar et sama;
himin hverfa   þau skulu hverjan dag
ǫldum at ártali.’
texts.translation:
“Mundilferi is he   who begat the moon,
And fathered the flaming sun;
The round of heaven   each day they run,
To tell the time for men.”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 23. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3265; bellows.txt line 4167). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 66, IA dieliederderlte00hild n89.

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 24
texts.original:
‘Seg þat et þriþja,   alls þik svinnan kveþa,
ef þú, Vafþrúþnir! vitir:
hvaþan dagr of kvam,   sás ferr drótt yfir,
eþa nǫ́tt meþ niþum?’
texts.translation:
“Third answer me well,   if wise thou art called,
If thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now:
Whence came the day,   o’er mankind that fares,
Or night with the narrowing moon?”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 24. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3274; bellows.txt line 4175). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 67, IA dieliederderlte00hild n90.

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 25
texts.original:
‘Dellingr heitir,   hann es Dags faþir,
en Nǫ́tt vas Nǫrvi borin;
ný ok niþ   skópu nýt regin
ǫldum at ártali.’
texts.translation:
“The father of day   is Delling called,
And the night was begotten by Nor;
Full moon and old   by the gods were fashioned,
To tell the time for men.”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 25. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3283; bellows.txt line 4199). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 67, IA dieliederderlte00hild n90.

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 26
texts.original:
‘Seg þat et fjórþa,   alls þik fróþan kveþa,
ef þú, Vafþrúþnir! vitir:
hvaþan vetr of kvam   eþa varmt sumar
fyrst meþ fróþ regin?’
texts.translation:
“Fourth answer me well,   if wise thou art called,
If thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now:
Whence did winter come,   or the summer warm,
First with the gracious gods?”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 26. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3292; bellows.txt line 4207). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 67, IA dieliederderlte00hild n90.

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 27
texts.original:
‘Vindsvalr heitir,   hann es Vetrar faþir,
en Svǫ́suþr Sumars’;
. . . . . . . .   . . . . . . . .
. . . . . . . . . .
texts.translation:
“Vindsval he was   who was winter’s father,
And Svosuth summer begat;”
. . . . . . . .   . . . . . . . .
. . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 27 (half lost; see Bellows' note 27). English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3301; bellows.txt line 4215). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 67, IA dieliederderlte00hild n90.

acquire.who: a weather-wise old seaman

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 28
texts.original:
‘Seg þat et fimta,   alls þik fróþan kveþa,
ef þú, Vafþrúþnir! vitir:
hverr jǫtna elztr   eþa Ymis niþja
yrþi í árdaga?’
texts.translation:
“Fifth answer me well,   if wise thou art called,
If thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now:
What giant first   was fashioned of old,
And the eldest of Ymir’s kin?”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 28. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3310; bellows.txt line 4247). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 68, IA dieliederderlte00hild n91.

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 29
texts.original:
‘Ørófi vetra,   áþr vǽri jǫrþ of skǫpuþ,
þá vas Bergelmir borinn;
Þrúþgelmir   vas þess faþir,
en Aurgelmir afi.’
texts.translation:
“Winters unmeasured   ere earth was made
Was the birth of Bergelmir;
Thruthgelmir’s son   was the giant strong,
And Aurgelmir’s grandson of old.”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 29. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3319; bellows.txt line 4255). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 68, IA dieliederderlte00hild n91.

acquire.who: a skald of the Svear king

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 30
texts.original:
‘Seg þat et sétta,   alls þik svinnan kveþa,
ef þú, Vafþrúþnir! vitir:
hvaþan Aurgelmir   kvam meþ jǫtna sunum
fyrst, enn fróþi jǫtunn?’
texts.translation:
“Sixth answer me well,   if wise thou art called,
If thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now:
Whence did Aurgelmir come   with the giants’ kin,
Long since, thou giant sage?”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 30. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3328; bellows.txt line 4263). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 68, IA dieliederderlte00hild n91.

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 31
texts.original:
‘Ór Élivǫ́gum   stukku eitrdropar,
svá óx unz ór varþ jǫtunn;
þar órar ǽttir   kvǫ́mu allar saman,
því’s þat ǽ allt til atalt.’
texts.translation:
“Down from Elivagar   did venom drop,
And waxed till a giant it was;
And thence arose   our giants’ race,
And thus so fierce are we found.”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 31. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3337; bellows.txt line 4271). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 pp. 68-69, IA dieliederderlte00hild n91-n92.

acquire.who: a skald at the king's seat

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 32
texts.original:
‘Seg þat et sjaunda,   alls þik svinnan kveþa,
ef þú, Vafþrúþnir! vitir:
hvé sá bǫrn of gat   enn baldni jǫtunn,
es hann hafþit gýgjar gaman?’
texts.translation:
“Seventh answer me well,   if wise thou art called,
If thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now:
How begat he children,   the giant grim,
Who never a giantess knew?”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 32. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3346; bellows.txt line 4300). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 69, IA dieliederderlte00hild n92.

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 33
texts.original:
‘Und hendi vaxa   kvǫ́þu hrímþursi
mey ok mǫg saman;
fótr viþ fǿti   gat ens fróþa jǫtuns
sexhǫfþaþan sun.’
texts.translation:
“They say ’neath the arms   of the giant of ice
Grew man-child and maid together;
And foot with foot   did the wise one fashion
A son that six heads bore.”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 33. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3355; bellows.txt line 4308). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 69, IA dieliederderlte00hild n92.

acquire.who: a skald

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 34
texts.original:
‘Seg þat et átta,   alls þik svinnan kveþa,
ef þú, Vafþrúþnir! vitir:
hvat fyrst of mant   eþa fremst of veizt?
þú ’st alsviþr, jǫtunn!’
texts.translation:
“Eighth answer me well,   if wise thou art called,
If thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now:
What farthest back   dost thou bear in mind?
For wide is thy wisdom, giant!”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 34. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3364; bellows.txt line 4316). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 69, IA dieliederderlte00hild n92.

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 35
texts.original:
‘Ørófi vetra   áþr vǽri jǫrþ of skǫpuþ,
þá vas Bergelmir borinn;
þat ek fyrst of man,   es sa enn fróþi jǫtunn
á vas lúþr of lagiþr.’
texts.translation:
“Winters unmeasured   ere earth was made
Was the birth of Bergelmir;
This first knew I well,   when the giant wise
In a boat of old was borne.”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 35. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3373; bellows.txt line 4342). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 70, IA dieliederderlte00hild n93.

acquire.who: a Gotland shipwright

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 36
texts.original:
‘Seg þat et niunda,   alls þik svinnan kveþa,
ef þú, Vafþrúþnir! vitir:
hvaþan vindr of kømr   sás ferr vág yfir?
ǽ menn hann sjalfan of sea.’
texts.translation:
“Ninth answer me well,   if wise thou art called,
If thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now:
Whence comes the wind   that fares o’er the waves
Yet never itself is seen?”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 36. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3382; bellows.txt line 4350). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 70, IA dieliederderlte00hild n93.

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 37
texts.original:
‘Hrǽsvelgr heitir   es sitr á himins enda,
jǫtunn í arnar ham;
af hans vǽngjum   kveþa vind koma
alla menn yfir.’
texts.translation:
“In an eagle’s guise   at the end of heaven
Hræsvelg sits, they say;
And from his wings   does the wind come forth
To move o’er the world of men.”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 37. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3391; bellows.txt line 4358). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 70, IA dieliederderlte00hild n93.

acquire.who: a Norse skipper you hail

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 38
texts.original:
‘Seg þat et tiunda,   alls þú tíva røk
ǫll, Vafþrúþnir! vitir:
hvaþan Njǫrþr of kvam   meþ niþjum ása —
[hofum ok hǫrgum   hann rǽþr hundmǫrgum] —
ok vasat hann ǫ́sum alinn?’
texts.translation:
“Tenth answer me now,   if thou knowest all
The fate that is fixed for the gods:
Whence came up Njorth   to the kin of the gods,—
(Rich in temples   and shrines he rules,—)
Though of gods he was never begot?”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 38. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3400; bellows.txt line 4366). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 70, IA dieliederderlte00hild n93.

texts.credit: English: Henry Adams Bellows, The Poetic Edda (New York, 1923). Old Norse: K. Hildebrand and H. Gering, Die Lieder der älteren Edda (Paderborn, 1904)

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 39
texts.original:
‘Í Vanaheimi   skópu hann vís regin
ok seldu at gíslingu goþum;
í aldar røk   hann mun aptr koma
heim meþ vísum vǫnum.’
texts.translation:
“In the home of the Wanes   did the wise ones create him,
And gave him as pledge to the gods;
At the fall of the world   shall he fare once more
Home to the Wanes so wise.”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 39. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3410; bellows.txt line 4394). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 71, IA dieliederderlte00hild n94.

acquire.who: a skald of the Svear king

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 40
texts.original:
‘Seg þat et ellifta,   alls þik svinnan kveþa,
ef þú, Vafþrúþnir! vitir:
hverir’u ýtar   es Óþins túnum í
hǫggvask hverjan dag?’
texts.translation:
“Eleventh answer me well,   . . . . . . . .
. . . . . . . . . . .
What men . . . . . .   in . . . . . . home
Each day to fight go forth?”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 40 (damaged in both manuscripts; in Hildebrand-Gering the words 'alls þik svinnan kveþa, ef þú, Vafþrúþnir! vitir', 'hverir’u' and 'es Óþins' are the editors' supplement, in italics). texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 41
texts.original:
‘Allir einherjar   Óþins túnum í
hǫggvask hverjan dag;
val þeir kjósa   ok ríþa vígi frá,
sitja meirr of sáttir saman.’
texts.translation:
“The heroes all   in Othin’s hall
Each day to fight go forth;
They fell each other,   and fare from the fight
All healed full soon to sit.”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 41. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3428; bellows.txt line 4411). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 71, IA dieliederderlte00hild n94.

acquire.who: the king's skald

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 42
texts.original:
‘Seg þat et tolfta,   hví þú tíva røk
ǫll, Vafþrúþnir! vitir?
frá jǫtna rúnum   ok allra goþa
segir þu et sannasta,
enn alsvinni jǫtunn!’
texts.translation:
“Twelfth answer me now   how all thou knowest
Of the fate that is fixed for the gods;
Of the runes of the gods   and the giants’ race
The truth indeed dost thou tell,
(And wide is thy wisdom, giant!)”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 42. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3437; bellows.txt line 4439). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 72, IA dieliederderlte00hild n95.

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 43
texts.original:
‘Frá jǫtna rúnum   ok allra goþa
ek kann segja satt,
þvít hvern hefk heim of komit:
niu kvamk heima   fyr Niflhel neþan,
hinig deyja [ór helju] halir.’
texts.translation:
“Of the runes of the gods   and the giants’ race
The truth indeed can I tell,
(For to every world have I won;)
To nine worlds came I,   to Niflhel beneath,
The home where dead men dwell.”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 43. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3447; bellows.txt line 4448). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 72, IA dieliederderlte00hild n95.

acquire.who: a Rus trader

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 44
texts.original:
‘Fjǫlþ ek fór,   fjǫlþ ek freistaþak,
fjǫlþ of reyndak regin:
hvat lifir manna,   þás enn mǽra líþr
fimbulvetr meþ firum?’
texts.translation:
“Much have I fared,   much have I found,
Much have I got of the gods:
What shall live of mankind   when at last there comes
The mighty winter to men?”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 44. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3457; bellows.txt line 4457). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 72, IA dieliederderlte00hild n95.

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 45
texts.original:
‘Líf ok Lífþrasir,   en þau leynask munu
í holti Hoddmimis;
morgindǫggvar   þau ser at mat hafa
en þaþan af aldir alask.’
texts.translation:
“In Hoddmimir’s wood   shall hide themselves
Lif and Lifthrasir then;
The morning dews   for meat shall they have,
Such food shall men then find.”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 45. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3466; bellows.txt line 4466). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 pp. 72-73, IA dieliederderlte00hild n95-n96.

acquire.who: a Skane farmer

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 46
texts.original:
‘Fjǫlþ ek fór,   fjǫlþ ek freistaþak,
fjǫlþ of reyndak regin:
hvaþan kømr sól   á enn slétta himin,
þás þessi hefr Fenrir farit?’
texts.translation:
“Much have I fared,   much have I found,
Much have I got of the gods:
Whence comes the sun   to the smooth sky back,
When Fenrir has snatched it forth?”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 46. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3475; bellows.txt line 4488). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 73, IA dieliederderlte00hild n96.

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 47
texts.original:
‘Eina dóttur   berr Alfrǫþull,
áþr henni Fenrir fari;
sú skal ríþa,   þás regin deyja,
móþur brautir mǽr.’
texts.translation:
“A daughter bright   Alfrothul bears
Ere Fenrir snatches her forth;
Her mother’s paths   shall the maiden tread
When the gods to death have gone.”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 47. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3484; bellows.txt line 4496). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 73, IA dieliederderlte00hild n96.

acquire.who: a Gotland stone-carver

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 48
texts.original:
‘Fjǫlþ ek fór,   fjǫlþ ek freistaþak,
fjǫlþ of reyndak regin:
hverjar ’u meyjar   es líþa mar yfir,
fróþgeþjaþar fara?’
texts.translation:
“Much have I fared,   much have I found,
Much have I got of the gods:
What maidens are they,   so wise of mind,
That forth o’er the sea shall fare?”

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 49
texts.original:
‘Þriar þjóþir   falla þorp yfir
meyja Mǫgþrasis,
hamingjur einar   þǽrs í heimi ’rú,
þó þǽr meþ jǫtnum alask.’
texts.translation:
“O’er Mogthrasir’s hill   shall the maidens pass,
And three are their throngs that come;
They all shall protect   the dwellers on earth,
Though they come of the giants’ kin.”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 49. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3502; bellows.txt line 4532). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 74, IA dieliederderlte00hild n97.

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 50
texts.original:
‘Fjǫlþ ek fór,   fjǫlþ ek freistaþak,
fjǫlþ of reyndak regin:
hverir ráþa ǽsir   eignum goþa,
þás sloknar Surta logi?’
texts.translation:
“Much have I fared,   much have I found,
Much have I got of the gods:
Who then shall rule   the realm of the gods,
When the fires of Surt have sunk?”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 50. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3511; bellows.txt line 4540). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 74, IA dieliederderlte00hild n97.

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 51
texts.original:
‘Víþarr ok Váli   byggva vé goþa,
þás sloknar Surta logi;
Móþi ok Magni   skulu Mjǫllni hafa
Vingnis at vígþroti.’
texts.translation:
“In the gods’ home Vithar   and Vali shall dwell,
When the fires of Surt have sunk;
Mothi and Magni   shall Mjollnir have
When Vingnir falls in fight.”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 51. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3520; bellows.txt line 4548). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 74, IA dieliederderlte00hild n97.

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 52
texts.original:
‘Fjǫlþ ek fór,   fjǫlþ ek freistaþak,
fjǫlþ of reyndak regin:
hvat verþr Óþni   at aldrlagi,
þás of rjúfask regin?’
texts.translation:
“Much have I fared,   much have I found,
Much have I got of the gods:
What shall bring the doom   of death to Othin,
When the gods to destruction go?”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 52. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3529; bellows.txt line 4556). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 74, IA dieliederderlte00hild n97.

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 53
texts.original:
‘Ulfr gleypa   mun Aldafǫþr,
þess mun Víþarr vreka;
kalda kjapta   hann klyfja mun
vitnis vígi at.’
texts.translation:
“The wolf shall fell   the father of men,
And this shall Vithar avenge;
The terrible jaws   shall he tear apart,
And so the wolf shall he slay.”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 53. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3538; bellows.txt line 4585). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 75, IA dieliederderlte00hild n98.

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 54
texts.original:
‘Fjǫlþ ek fór,   fjǫlþ ek freistaþak,
fjǫlþ of reyndak regin:
hvat mǽlti Óþinn,   áþr á bál stigi,
sjalfr í eyra syni?’
texts.translation:
“Much have I fared,   much have I found,
Much have I got from the gods:
What spake Othin himself   in the ears of his son,
Ere in the bale-fire he burned?”
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 54. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3547; bellows.txt line 4593). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 75, IA dieliederderlte00hild n98.

texts.title: Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 55
texts.original:
‘Ey manni þat veit,   hvat þu í árdaga
sagþir í eyra syni:
feigum munni   mǽltak mína forna stafi
auk of ragna røk.
Nú viþ Óþin   deildak orþspeki,
þú’st ǽ vísastr vera.’
texts.where: Vafþrúðnismál st. 55. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 3556; bellows.txt line 4601). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 75, IA dieliederderlte00hild n98.

texts.title: Alvis's lay, stanza 9
texts.original:
Seg mer þat, Alvíss!   ǫll of røk fira
vǫrumk, dvergr! at vitir:
hvé sú jǫrþ heitir,   es liggr fyr alda sunum,
heimi hverjum í?’
texts.translation:
“Answer me, Alvis!   thou knowest all,
Dwarf, of the doom of men:
What call they the earth,   that lies before all,
In each and every world?”
texts.where: Alvíssmál st. 9 (Thor's speech runs on from st. 8, so no opening quote in the Norse). texts.title: Alvis's lay, stanza 10
texts.original:
‘Jǫrþ heitir meþ mǫnnum,   en meþ ǫ́sum fold,
kalla vega vanir,
ígrǿn jǫtnar,   alfar groandi,
kalla aur uppregin.’
texts.translation:
“‘Earth’ to men, ‘Field’   to the gods it is,
‘The Ways’ is it called by the Wanes;
‘Ever Green’ by the giants,   ‘The Grower’ by elves,
‘The Moist’ by the holy ones high.”
texts.where: Alvíssmál st. 10. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 7751; bellows.txt line 9332). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 156, IA dieliederderlte00hild n179.

texts.title: Alvis's lay, stanza 11
texts.original:
‘Seg mer þat, Alvíss!   ǫll of røk fira
vǫrumk, dvergr! at vitir:
hvé sá himinn heitir   † erakendi,
heimi hverjum í?’
texts.translation:
“Answer me, Alvis!   thou knowest all,
Dwarf, of the doom of men:
What call they the heaven,   beheld of the high one,
In each and every world?”

texts.title: Alvis's lay, stanza 12
texts.original:
‘Himinn heitir meþ mǫnnum,   en hlyrnir meþ goþum,
kalla vindofni vanir,
uppheim jǫtnar,   alfar fagra rǽfr,
dvergar drjúpan sal.’
texts.translation:
“‘Heaven’ men call it,   ‘The Height’ the gods,
The Wanes ‘The Weaver of Winds’;
Giants ‘The Up-World,’   elves ‘The Fair-Roof,’
The dwarfs ‘The Dripping Hall.’”
texts.where: Alvíssmál st. 12. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 7769; bellows.txt line 9369). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 pp. 156-157, IA dieliederderlte00hild n179-n180.

texts.title: Alvis's lay, stanza 13
texts.original:
‘Seg mer þat, Alvíss!   ǫll of røk fira
vǫrumk, dvergr! at vitir:
hversu máni heitir,   sás menn sea,
heimi hverjum í?’
texts.translation:
“Answer me, Alvis!   thou knowest all,
Dwarf, of the doom of men:
What call they the moon,   that men behold,
In each and every world?”

texts.title: Alvis's lay, stanza 14
texts.original:
‘Máni heitir meþ mǫnnum,   en mylinn meþ goþum,
kalla hvél helju í,
skyndi jǫtnar,   en skin dvergar,
kalla alfar ártala.’
texts.translation:
“‘Moon’ with men, ‘Flame’   the gods among,
‘The Wheel’ in the house of hell;
‘The Goer’ the giants,   ‘The Gleamer’ the dwarfs,
The elves ‘The Teller of Time.’”
texts.where: Alvíssmál st. 14. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 7787; bellows.txt line 9410). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 157, IA dieliederderlte00hild n180.

texts.title: Alvis's lay, stanza 15
texts.original:
‘Seg mer þat, Alvíss!   ǫll of røk fira
vǫrumk, dvergr! at vitir:
hvé sú sól heitir,   es sea alda synir,
heimi hverjum í?’
texts.translation:
“Answer me, Alvis!   thou knowest all,
Dwarf, of the doom of men:
What call they the sun,   that all men see,
In each and every world?”

texts.title: Alvis's lay, stanza 16
texts.original:
‘Sól heitir meþ mǫnnum,   en sunna meþ goþum,
kalla dvergar Dvalins leika,
eygló jǫtnar,   alfar fagra hvél,
alskír ása synir.’
texts.translation:
“Men call it ‘Sun,’   gods ‘Orb of the Sun,’
‘The Deceiver of Dvalin’ the dwarfs;
The giants ‘The Ever-Bright,’   elves ‘Fair Wheel,’
‘All-Glowing’ the sons of the gods.”
texts.where: Alvíssmál st. 16. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 7805; bellows.txt line 9428). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 157, IA dieliederderlte00hild n180.

texts.original:
‘Seg mer þat, Alvíss!   ǫll of røk fira
vǫrumk, dvergr! at vitir:
hvé þau ský heita,   es skúrum blandask,
heimi hverjum í?’
texts.translation:
“Answer me, Alvis!   thou knowest all,
Dwarf, of the doom of men:
What call they the clouds,   that keep the rains,
In each and every world?”

texts.original:
‘Ský heita meþ mǫnnum,   en skúrvǫ́n meþ goþum,
kalla vindflot vanir,
úrvǫ́n jǫtnar,   alfar veþrmegin,
kalla í helju hjalm huliþs.’
texts.translation:
“‘Clouds’ men name them,   ‘Rain-Hope’ gods call them,
The Wanes call them ‘Kites of the Wind’;
‘Water-Hope’ giants,   ‘Weather-Might’ elves,
‘The Helmet of Secrets’ in hell.”
texts.where: Alvíssmál st. 18. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 7823; bellows.txt line 9460). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 158, IA dieliederderlte00hild n181.

texts.original:
‘Seg mer þat, Alvíss!   ǫll of røk fira
vǫrumk, dvergr! at vitir:
hvé sá vindr heitir,   es víþast ferr,
heimi hverjum í?’
texts.translation:
“Answer me, Alvis!   thou knowest all,
Dwarf, of the doom of men:
What call they the wind,   that widest fares,
In each and every world?”

texts.title: Alvis's lay, stanza 20
texts.original:
‘Vindr heitir meþ mǫnnum,   en vǫ́fuþr meþ goþum,
kalla gneggjuþ ginnregin,
ǿpi jǫtnar,   alfar dynfara,
kalla í helju hviþuþ.’
texts.translation:
“‘Wind’ do men call it,   the gods ‘The Waverer,’
‘The Neigher’ the holy ones high;
‘The Wailer’ the giants,   ‘Roaring Wender’ the elves,
In hell ‘The Blustering Blast.’”
texts.where: Alvíssmál st. 20 (also quoted by Snorri, Skáldskaparmál). English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 7841; bellows.txt line 9477). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 158, IA dieliederderlte00hild n181.

texts.title: Alvis's lay, stanza 21
texts.original:
‘Seg mer þat, Alvíss!   ǫll of røk fira
vǫrumk, dvergr! at vitir:
hvé þat logn heitir,   es liggja skal,
heimi hverjum í?’
texts.translation:
“Answer me, Alvis!   thou knowest all,
Dwarf, of the doom of men:
What call they the calm,   that quiet lies,
In each and every world?”

texts.title: Alvis's lay, stanza 22
texts.original:
‘Logn heitir meþ mǫnnum,   en lǿgi meþ goþum,
kalla vindslot vanir,
ofhlý jǫtnar,   alfar dagsefa,
kalla dvergar dags veru.’
texts.translation:
“‘Calm’ men call it,   ‘The Quiet’ the gods,
The Wanes ‘The Hush of the Winds’;
‘The Sultry’ the giants,   elves ‘Day’s Stillness,’
The dwarfs ‘The Shelter of Day.’”
texts.where: Alvíssmál st. 22. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 7859; bellows.txt line 9513). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 159, IA dieliederderlte00hild n182.

texts.title: Alvis's lay, stanza 23
texts.original:
‘Seg mer þat, Alvíss!   ǫll of røk fira
vǫrumk, dvergr! at vitir:
hvé sá marr heitir,   es menn roa,
heimi hverjum í?’
texts.translation:
“Answer me, Alvis!   thou knowest all,
Dwarf, of the doom of men:
What call they the sea,   whereon men sail,
In each and every world?”

texts.title: Alvis's lay, stanza 24
texts.original:
‘Sǽr heitir meþ mǫnnum,   en sílǽgja meþ goþum,
kalla vág vanir,
álheim jǫtnar,   alfar lágastaf,
kalla dvergar djúpan mar.’
texts.translation:
“‘Sea’ men call it,   gods ‘The Smooth-Lying,’
‘The Wave’ is it called by the Wanes;
‘Eel-Home’ the giants,   ‘Drink-Stuff’ the elves,
For the dwarfs its name is ‘The Deep.’”
texts.where: Alvíssmál st. 24. English: Bellows 1923, Gutenberg #73533 (m2/pg73533.txt line 7877; bellows.txt line 9529). Old Norse: Hildebrand-Gering 1904 p. 159, IA dieliederderlte00hild n182.

texts.title: Alvis's lay, stanza 25
texts.original:
‘Seg mer þat, Alvíss!   ǫll of røk fira
vǫrumk, dvergr! at vitir:
hvé sá eldr heitir,   es brinnr fyr alda sunum,
heimi hverjum í?’
texts.translation:
“Answer me, Alvis!   thou knowest all,
Dwarf, of the doom of men:
What call they the fire,   that flames for men,
In each of all the worlds?”

texts.original:
‘Eldr heitir meþ mǫnnum,   en meþ ǫ́sum funi,
kalla vǽgin vanir,
freka jǫtnar,   en forbrenni dvergar,
kalla í helju hrǫþuþ.’
texts.translation:
“‘Fire’ men call it,   and ‘Flame’ the gods,
By the Wanes is it ‘Wildfire’ called;
‘The Biter’ by giants,   ‘The Burner’ by dwarfs,
‘The Swift’ in the house of hell.”

vǫrumk, dvergr! at vitir:

heimi hverjum í?’

In each and every world?”

kalla hlíþþang halir,
eldi jǫtnar,   alfar fagrlima,
kalla vǫnd vanir.’
texts.translation:

‘Seaweed of Hills’ in hell;
‘Flame-Food’ the giants,   ‘Fair-Limbed’ the elves,
‘The Wand’ is it called by the Wanes.”

texts.original:
‘Nǫ́tt heitir meþ mǫnnum,   en njól meþ goþum,

óljós jǫtnar,   alfar svefngaman,
kalla dvergar draumnjǫrun.’

‘The Hood’ the holy ones high;

texts.title: Exeter Book riddle (storm set, part 1)
texts.original:
Hwylc is hæleþa þæs horsc   ond þæs hygecræftig
þæt þæt mæge asecgan,   hwa mec on sið wræce,
þonne ic astige strong,   stundum reþe
þrymful þunie?   þragum wræc(c)a
fere geond foldan,   folcsalo bærne,
ræced reafige,   recas stigað
haswe ofer hrofum,   hlin bið on eorþan,
wælcwealm wera.   þonne ic wudu hrere,
bearwas bledhwate,   beamas fylle,
holme gehrefed,   heahum meahtum
wrecan on waþe,   wide sended;
hæbbe me on hrycge   þæt ær hadas wreah
foldbuendra,   flæsc ond gæstas,
somod on sonde.   Saga, hwa mec þecce,
oþþe hu ic hatte,   þe þa hlæst bere.
texts.translation:
What man is so sagacious,
and of mind so cunning,
that that may say,
who me on journey sends,
when I mount strong,
sometimes fierce,
proud, I thunder.
at times wander,
travel over earth,
public structures burn,
houses rob;
the smoke mounts
dusky o'er the roofs;
din is on earth,
the death-pang of men.
Then I shake the wood,
the leafy groves,
fell the trees,
with water cover'd,
by my high powers,
exiles wandering
send afar.
I have on my back
that which ere the persons cover'd
of earth's inhabitants,
flesh and spirits,
together safely.
Say who covers me,
or how I am call'd
who bear the load.
texts.where: Old English: F. Tupper, The Riddles of the Exeter Book (Boston 1910), Riddle 2, p. 2 (Internet Archive riddlesofexeterbook00tuppuoft; file scratchpad\m2\riddlesofexeterbook00tuppuoft.txt lines 5687-5707). English: B. Thorpe, Codex Exoniensis (London 1842), Riddle II, pp. 380-381 (Internet Archive cu31924013337617; file scratchpad\thorpe_exon.txt lines 49230-49327; checked against Internet Archive codexexoniensisc00sociuoft, file scratchpad\m2\codexexoniensisc00sociuoft.txt). Krapp & Dobbie number: Riddle 1 (reference only). Manuscript: Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501, fol. 101a.

texts.title: Exeter Book riddle (storm set, part 2)
texts.original:
Hwilum ic gewite,   swa ne wenaþ men,
under yþa geþræc   eorþan secan,
garsecges grund.   Gifen biþ gewreged,
fam gewealcen;
hwælmere hlimmeð,   hlude grimmeð;
streamas staþu beatað,   stundum weorpaþ
on stealc hleoþa   stane ond sonde,
ware ond wæge,   þonne ic winnende,
holmmægne biþeaht,   hrusan styrge,
side sægrundas:   sundhelme ne mæg
losian ær mec læte,   se þe min latteow bið
on siþa gehwam.   Saga, þoncol mon,
hwa mec bregde   of brimes fæþmum,
þonne streamas eft   stille weorþað,
yþa geþwære,   þe mec ær wrugon.
texts.translation:
Sometimes I go,
as men think not,
under the rush of waves,
seeking the earth,
the ocean's ground.
The sea is impel'd,
foam roll'd;
the whale-mere resounds,
loud rages,
streams beat the shores,
sometimes dash,
on the * cliffs,
with stone and sand,
weed and wave:
then I labouring,
with the watery main cover'd,
the earth stir up,
the wide sea-grounds.
From the watery covering I may not
escape, ere me dismiss
he who my guide is
in every course.
Say, man of thought!
who me drew
from ocean's bosom,
when the streams again
were still,
the waves at rest,
which me ere cover'd?
texts.where: Old English: Tupper 1910, Riddle 3, pp. 2-3 (riddlesofexeterbook00tuppuoft; scratchpad\m2\riddlesofexeterbook00tuppuoft.txt lines 5709-5751). English: Thorpe 1842, Riddle III, pp. 381-382 (cu31924013337617; scratchpad\thorpe_exon.txt lines 49330-49433). Krapp & Dobbie Riddle 2.

texts.title: Exeter Book riddle (storm set, part 3)
texts.original:
Hwilum mec min frea   fæste genearwað,
sendeð þonne   under sælwonge
bearm [þone] bradan   ond on bid wriceð,
þrafað on þystrum   þrymma sumne,
hæste on enge,   þær me heard siteð
hruse on hrycge:   nah ic hwyrftweges
of þam aglace,   ac ic eþelstol
hæleþa hrere:   hornsalu wagiað,
wera wicstede;   weallas beofiað,
steape ofer stiwitum.   Stille þynceð
lyft ofer londe   ond lagu swige,
oþþæt ic of enge   up aþringe,
efne swa mec wisaþ   se mec wræde on
æt frumsceafte   furþum legde
bende ond clomme,   þæt ic onbugan ne mot
of þæs gewealde   þe me wegas tæcneð.
Hwilum ic sceal ufan   yþa wregan,
[streamas] styrgan   ond to staþe þywan
flintgrægne flod:   famig winneð
wæg wið wealle;   wonn ariseð
dun ofer dype,   hyre deorc on last,
eare geblonden,   oþer fereð,
þæt hy gemittað   mearclonde neah
hea hlincas.   þær bið hlud wudu,
brimgiesta breahtm;   bidað stille
stealc stanhleoþu   streamgewinnes,
hopgehnastes,   þonne heah geþring
on cleofu crydeð:   þær bið ceole wen
sliþre sæcce,   gif hine sæ byreð
on þa grimman tid,   gæsta fulne,
þæt he scyle rice   birofen weorþan,
feore bifohten   fæmig ridan
yþa hrycgum:   þær bið egsa sum
hæleþum geywed,   þara þe ic hyran sceal
strong on stiðweg:   hwa gestilleð þæt?
Hwilum ic þurhræse   þæt me rideð on bæce,
won wægfatu,   wide toþringe
lagustreama full,   hwilum læte eft
slupan tosomne.   Se bið swega mæst,
breahtma ofer burgum,   ond gebreca hludast,
þonne scearp cymeð   sceor wið oþrum,
ecg wið ecge:   eorþan gesceafte
fus ofer folcum   fyre swætað,
blacan lige,   ond gebrecu ferað
deorc ofer dreohtum   gedyne micle,
farað feohtende,   feallan lætað
sweart sumsendu   seaw of bosme,
wætan of wombe.   Winnende fareð
atol eoredþreat,   egsa astigeð,
micel modþrea   monna cynne,
brogan on burgum,   þonne blace scotiað
scriþende scin   scearpum wæpnum.
Dol him ne ondrædeð   ða deaðsperu,
swylteð hwæþre,   gif him soð meotud
on geryhtu   þurh regn ufan
of gestune læteð   stræle fleogan,
ferende flan:   fea þæt gedygað
þara þe geræceð   rynegiestes wæpen.
Ic þæs orleges   or anstelle,
þonne gewite   wolcengehnaste
þurh geþræc þringan   þrimme micle
ofer byrnan bosm:   biersteð hlude
heah hloðgecrod;   þonne hnige eft
under lyfte helm   londe near
ond me [on] hrycg hlade   þæt ic habban sceal,
meahtum gemanad   mines frean.
Swa ic, þrymful þeow,   þragum winne,
hwilum under eorþan,   hwilum yþa sceal
hean underhnigan,   hwilum holm ufan
streamas styrge,   hwilum stige up,
wolcnfare wrege,   wide fere
swift ond swiþfeorm.   Saga hwæt ic hatte,
oþþe hwa mec rære   þonne ic restan ne mot,
oþþe hwa mec stæðþe   þonne ic stille beom.
texts.translation:
Sometimes me my master
fast constrains,
then sends,
amid the pleasant plain,
my broad bosom,
and on a bed drives me,
urges on in darkness
some affliction,
hunts me into durance;
there hard sits
the earth on my back.
I have no return of way
from that misery;
but I the habitation
of men disturb,
the pinnacled halls shake,
men's dwelling-places,
the walls tremble,
steep o'er the pathways;
still seems
the air o'er the land,
and the water silent,
till that I from durance
rush up,
just as me directs
he who a binding on me,
at the beginning,
first laid,
with band and chain,
that I may not deviate
from the control of him,
who to me points the ways.
Sometimes I shall from above
the billows drive,
stir up the streams,
and to the shore impel
the flint-gray flood.
Foamy strives
wave against wall,
dusk rises
mountain o'er deep;
dark on its track,
in ocean,
another goes,
so that they meet,
the land's limit near,
the high shores.
There the wood is loud,
the ocean-guests' noise;
still remain
the rocky cliffs
from the watery strife,
the crew's outcry.
When the towering mass
on the cliffs presses,
there shall be hope for the vessel,
in the fierce contest,
if it the sea shall bear,
at that terrific time,
of guests full,
so that it shall forthwith
be borne away,
though vitally assail'd,
yet foamy ride
on the waves' backs.
There shall be some terror
to men display'd,
whom I shall hear,
strong on the rugged way:
who shall still that?
Sometimes I rush through,
so that behind me rides
the dark wave-vessel;
widely I press on,
of the water-streams full:
sometimes again I let them
dissolve together;
that of sounds is greatest,
of noises among men,
and of crashes loudest.
Then sharp shall come
shoe against other,
edge against edge,
to earth's creation,
hurrying o'er people;
they with fire shall sweat,
with pale flame,
and the crashes go
dark over multitudes;
with great din,
they shall go fighting,
shall let fall,
swart shall send,
moisture from the bosom,
liquid from the belly;
contending shall go
the dire legion,
dread shall arise,
great mental torment,
to the race of men,
terror in their towns,
when pale shall shoot
passing phantoms
with sharp weapons,
the foolish will not dread
the deadly spears,
yet will he die,
if on him the just Creator
righteously,
through rain from above,
from the whirlwind lets
the arrow fly,
the travelling dart:
few shall from that escape
of those whom reach
the rain-spirit's weapon.
I of that calamity
set the beginning,
then depart
in the din of clouds,
boldly pressing onward
with a great state,
o'er the water's bosom;
loud bursts
the high collection.
Then I incline again,
under air's covering,
nearer to land,
and on my back load
what I am to have,
by the powers admonish'd
of my master.
So I a stately servant,
at times labour,
sometimes under earth;
sometimes the waves I must
deep dive under;
sometimes the sea from above,
the streams, I agitate;
sometimes rise up,
the clouds' course drive,
widely traverse,
swift and vigorous.
Say what I am call'd,
or who excites me,
when I may not rest,
or who stays me,
when I am still?

texts.title: Exeter Book riddle 5
texts.original:
Ic eom anhaga   iserne wund,
bille gebennad,   beadoweorca sæd,
ecgum werig.   Oft ic wig seo,
frecne feohtan,   frofre ne wene,
þæt me geoc cyme   guðgewinnes,
ær ic mid ældum   eal forwurde;
ac mec hnossiað   homera lafe,
heardecg heoroscearp,   hondweorc smiþa,
bitað in burgum;   ic abidan sceal
laþran gemotes.   Næfre læcecynn
on folcstede   findan meahte,
þara þe mid wyrtum   wunde gehælde,
ac me ecga dolg   eacen weorðað
þurh deaðslege   dagum ond nihtum.
texts.translation:
I am a recluse,
with iron wounded,
with faulchion scar'd,
sated with works of war,
of edges weary;
oft I battle see,
perilous fight;
for comfort hope not,
or that safety to me shall come
from martial strife,
ere I with generations
shall all have perish'd;
but they me shall strike
with sword:
the hard of edge, intensely sharp,
hand-work of smiths,
shall bite among people:
I must await
the hostile meeting:
never the healing tribe,
in the battle-place,
might I find,
who with plants
my wounds would heal,
but to me the edges' sores
become increas'd,
through deadly stroke,
by day and night.
texts.where: Old English: Tupper 1910, Riddle 6, p. 7 (scratchpad\m2\riddlesofexeterbook00tuppuoft.txt lines 5981-6009). English: Thorpe 1842, Riddle VI, p. 388 (scratchpad\thorpe_exon.txt lines 50088-50172). Krapp & Dobbie Riddle 5.
